title: A Roman birthday party invitation from around AD 100 still survives

cover.alt: A long glass display case at the British Museum with rows of dark, thin fragments of Roman wooden writing tablets from Vindolanda laid out on white mounts.

body: Vindolanda was a Roman fort in northern Britain, and its soldiers and their families wrote letters and accounts in carbon ink on thin wooden leaves about the size of a postcard. Written in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, they lasted because the ground there kept out oxygen, and archaeologists began digging them up in 1973. One, **tablet 291**, is an invitation from Claudia Severa, the wife of a nearby fort’s commander, asking Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of the prefect Flavius Cerialis, to her birthday party. A scribe wrote most of it, but Severa added the closing greeting herself, which makes it one of the earliest known examples of Latin written by a woman.

slides.alt: Two thin, cracked wooden leaves side by side, covered in faded lines of Roman cursive handwriting in dark ink: Vindolanda tablet 291.
slides.caption: Tablet 291, written around AD 100. The letter runs across two wooden leaves; most of it is in a scribe’s hand, the final greeting in Claudia Severa’s own.

slides.prompt: When the excavators first saw the tablets in the mud, what did they think they were?
slides.detail: Then one of the diggers found two pieces stuck together, with writing inside. Infrared photographs later made the faded ink readable.

slides.heading: Nineteen centuries in the ground
slides.note: Nearly 500 of the tablets were dug up in the 1970s and 1980s.

slides.heading: Also in the tablets
items: A letter listing socks, two pairs of sandals and two pairs of underpants
The biggest group: letters of the prefect Flavius Cerialis

slides.clue: The Roman garrison’s patronising nickname for the local people, meaning ‘little Britons’
slides.detail: A diminutive of Britto, a Briton. Roman garrisons in northern Britain used it, patronisingly, for the people around them.
